Congenital Heart Disease

cyanotic lesions · left-to-right shunts · ductal-dependent lesions · pulse oximetry screen · tet spells · timing: days for the ductus, weeks for shuntsWhen did it declare, and which structure makes the murmur?

1Illness script
Bottom line
  • Cyanosis within hours of birth that 100% oxygen does not fix is a right-to-left shunt (the 5 Ts); a holosystolic murmur by 2 to 3 weeks (moderate defect) and heart failure by 4 to 6 weeks (larger defect) is a left-to-right shunt.
  • A newborn in shock as the ductus closes gets prostaglandin E1 (PGE1) before echocardiography; a preterm ductus flooding the lungs with respiratory compromise can sometimes be closed with indomethacin or ibuprofen.
  • Tetralogy of Fallot (tet) spell: cyanosis deepens and the murmur fades with crying; knee-chest position and oxygen first, then morphine, fluids, phenylephrine or propranolol may help.
What it is

Structural heart lesions sorted by shunt direction: right to left (cyanotic: the 5 Ts, which are truncus arteriosus, transposition, tricuspid atresia, tetralogy of Fallot and total anomalous pulmonary venous return; Ebstein anomaly; hypoplastic left heart), left to right (septal defects, patent ductus arteriosus) or obstruction (coarctation).

Driver

A murmur needs a pressure gradient, and blood takes the lower resistance: the balance of pulmonary and systemic resistance sets each shunt and when it declares.

Triggers

: atrioventricular septal defect

non-modifiable

;

: truncus arteriosus, tetralogy

non-modifiable

; Turner syndrome: coarctation

non-modifiable

; maternal diabetes: transposition

; maternal lithium: Ebstein anomaly

; fetal alcohol: tetralogy

; congenital rubella, prematurity and respiratory distress syndrome: patent ductus arteriosus

Chain

At birth pulmonary resistance is high, so little crosses a septal defect

resistance falls over weeks; the left-to-right shunt and its murmur grow

overcirculation brings heart failure by 4 to 6 weeks

left unrepaired, pulmonary resistance often rises and the shunt reverses: Eisenmenger syndrome

Insights

The murmur tracks the gradient: a small ventricular defect is loud and a large one quiet; in tetralogy the large septal defect is usually silent and the murmur is the narrowed outflow tract, so it fades as a spell tightens it.

Ductal-dependent lesions stay hidden until the ductus constricts at about 24 to 72 hours, and the pulse oximetry screen is done at 24 hours or later.

Hourstransposition: severe cyanosis; obstructed venous return: pulmonary edema

By day 10critical coarctation in shock

2Urgent risks
Act now
FindingAction
Newborn with weak pulses, pallor or shock in the first daysDuctal-dependent lesion: start PGE1 now; echocardiography follows.
Hypoplastic left heart on PGE1Give as little oxygen as possible: oxygen lowers pulmonary resistance and steals systemic flow.
Tet spell: deeper cyanosis with crying, a fading murmurKnee-chest position and oxygen; morphine, fluids, phenylephrine or propranolol may help.
Cyanosis with pulmonary edema shortly after birthObstructed total anomalous pulmonary venous return: emergent surgical repair.
Transposition still hypoxemic on PGE1Balloon atrial septostomy.
3Differential

Sort lung from heart and airway first in ; for a murmur in a well child, see .

Cyanotic lesions
LesionDecides itNext best step
Transposition of the great arteriesWithin hours of birth: severe cyanosis, no murmur, single loud second heart sound (S2); egg on a string.Start PGE1; arterial switch, typically in the first week.
Total anomalous pulmonary venous returnAt birth: pulmonary veins drain to the right heart, so survival needs an atrial defect; no significant murmur; obstructed drainage brings pulmonary edema.Echocardiography; emergent repair if obstructed.
Hypoplastic left heart syndromeFirst 24 to 48 hours: shock as the ductus closes; no murmur.Start PGE1 with minimal oxygen; plan staged operations.
Tricuspid atresiaAt birth: no tricuspid valve and a small right ventricle; cyanosis, a septal defect murmur, left axis deviation.Start PGE1 if severe; plan staged operations.
Truncus arteriosusFirst weeks: usually mild cyanosis with heart failure; one arterial trunk over a ventricular septal defect; 22q11.2 deletion in about 35%.Treat the failure; early surgical repair; check calcium and T cells.
Tetralogy of FallotSpells peak at 2 to 4 months: the most common cyanotic lesion; harsh systolic ejection murmur, left upper sternal border; boot-shaped heart.Echocardiography; repair at 2 to 6 months, earlier if symptoms are severe.
Ebstein anomalyAt birth if severe: tricuspid leaflets displaced into the right ventricle; regurgitation, widely split first heart sound (S1), a massive heart; maternal lithium.Obtain echocardiography; start PGE1 when severely cyanotic.
Left-to-right shunts and obstruction
LesionDecides itNext best step
Ventricular septal defectModerate defect: murmur by 2 to 3 weeks; larger defect: failure by 4 to 6: this is the most common lesion in infancy; holosystolic, left lower sternal border; louder means smaller.Diuretics and feeding; surgical closure if failure persists.
Complete atrioventricular septal defect (atrioventricular canal)Down syndrome; heart failure by 4 to 6 weeks; single loud S2.Echocardiography; repair by 2 to 4 months.
Atrial septal defectOften silent into childhood: fixed split S2, soft ejection murmur; no cyanosis.Obtain echocardiography; small central defects often close.
Patent ductus arteriosusCommon in preterm infants: continuous machine-like murmur; bounding pulses and wide pulse pressure with a significant shunt.Preterm with compromise: give indomethacin or ibuprofen.
Coarctation of the aortaDays 1 to 10: weak femoral pulses, arm pressure above leg; Turner syndrome, bicuspid aortic valve.PGE1 when symptomatic; then repair.
Isolated pulmonary stenosisSystolic ejection murmur radiating to the back; no septal defect, so no cyanotic spells.Obtain echocardiography.
Eisenmenger syndromeYears after an unrepaired shunt: late cyanosis, clubbing, polycythemia; a reversed ductus turns only the legs blue.Prevent by timely repair; once established, transplantation.

Clues that change the answer
CluePoints toNext best step

Saturation falls to 60% and the murmur fades while cryingTet spell: less outflow, less murmurPlace him knee to chest and give oxygen.

Fixed split S2, no cyanosisAtrial septal defectObtain echocardiography.
Pause point
Tetralogy spell A softer murmur read as improvement A softer tetralogy murmur during a spell means less pulmonary flow → Not improvement
5Diagnostic criteria
Positive pulse oximetry screen (24 hours or later)
MeasurementPositive if
Any single readingUnder 90%
Right hand and footBoth under 95% on repeat checks 1 hour apart
Hand-foot differenceOver 3% on repeat paired checks 1 hour apart
Tetralogy of Fallot: four components (PROVe)
ComponentConsequence
Pulmonary infundibular stenosisSets the shunt and makes the murmur
Right ventricular hypertrophyFollows the outflow obstruction
Overriding aortaSits directly over the defect
Ventricular septal defectLarge, so it makes no murmur
6Severity
What the ductus supplies
GroupLesionsMeaning
Ductal-dependent pulmonary flowSevere tetralogy, tricuspid atresia, severe Ebstein anomalyPGE1 keeps the ductus open; cyanosis deepens as it closes
Ductal-dependent systemic flowHypoplastic left heart, critical coarctationPGE1 before echocardiography; shock as it closes

Not ductal-dependentSeptal defects; a preterm patent ductusOvercirculation; a symptomatic preterm ductus is closed
7Treatment
1

Ductal-dependentCyanosis or shock as the ductus closes

PGE1 (alprostadil) infusion; minimal oxygen in hypoplastic left heart.

2

Tet spellDeep cyanosis with crying

Knee-chest position and oxygen; morphine, fluids, phenylephrine or propranolol may help; ketamine, intubation or surgery if refractory. It raises systemic vascular resistance, so less blood crosses right to left.

3

After a spellUnrepaired tetralogy

Oral propranolol until repair; one significant spell calls for prompt surgery.

4

Shunt failureHeart failure at 4 to 6 weeks

Diuretics, digoxin or an angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor to control the failure, with fortified feeds; surgical closure if failure or poor growth persists.

5

Preterm ductusSignificant shunt with respiratory compromise

Indomethacin or ibuprofen; typically no treatment without compromise.

6

DefinitiveOnce stable

Arterial switch, typically in the first week, for transposition; tetralogy repair at 2 to 6 months, earlier if symptoms are severe; staged operations for hypoplastic left heart and tricuspid atresia.

8Follow-up
After diagnosis or repair
WhenDo
Small ventricular septal defect, under 5 mmObserve; small defects often close in the first few years.
Unrepaired large shunt with a softening murmurUrgent cardiology review: pulmonary resistance may be rising, the road to Eisenmenger syndrome.
After repairEndocarditis prophylaxis for 6 months, longer with a residual defect beside a patch; see .
After tetralogy repairWatch for pulmonic regurgitation.
Ebstein anomalyECG for Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome, present in 20%.
Practice
  1. 5-week-old boy, born at term, had a normal 2-week visit now feeds poorly and breathes fast new holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border Murmur absent on the newborn examination Afebrile · respiratory rate 70/min · acyanotic → Pulmonary vascular resistance has fallen → at birth pulmonary vascular resistance is near systemic, so almost nothing crosses the defect; as it falls, the gradient opens, the murmur appears by 2 to 3 weeks, and the same overcirculation causes the tachypnea and poor feeding. The ductus was already closed by the normal 2-week visit, and its closure removes a continuous murmur rather than creating a holosystolic one; rising pulmonary pressure would soften the murmur
  2. 1-day-old boy has been cyanotic since birth no murmur echocardiogram shows the pulmonary veins draining to the right atrium Born at term after an uncomplicated pregnancy Afebrile · oxygen saturation 80% on room air · HR 160/min → Total anomalous pulmonary venous return → pulmonary veins draining to the right heart give cyanosis at birth with no murmur, at most a soft pulmonic flow murmur; tetralogy has a harsh outflow murmur, and truncus arteriosus has a holosystolic murmur with cyanosis typically arriving in infancy
  3. 6-week-old boy was diagnosed with a large ventricular septal defect at 2 weeks poor weight gain liver edge 3 cm below the costal margin Feeds tire him Afebrile · respiratory rate 70/min → Diuretics, afterload reduction and caloric fortification → heart failure from a left-to-right shunt arrives at 4 to 6 weeks; failure to thrive is the infant form of exercise intolerance. Diurese and feed first, and close the defect if failure persists: observation leaves the failure untreated, and surgery comes after medical therapy fails
  4. 4-month-old boy has episodes of deep cyanosis while crying episodes resolve when he is held with knees to chest harsh systolic murmur at the left upper sternal border Afebrile · oxygen saturation 84% between episodes → Tetralogy of Fallot → right ventricular outflow tract obstruction drives right-to-left flow across a large ventricular septal defect, and knee-chest raises systemic vascular resistance to reverse it; truncus arteriosus gives a holosystolic murmur without spells, and total anomalous pulmonary venous return has no murmur
  5. 1-day-old girl has a normal examination before discharge fails her pulse oximetry screen at 24 hours Born at term after an uncomplicated pregnancy; feeding well Afebrile · HR 140/min · BP 70/42 mm Hg → Echocardiography → a failed screen means possible critical congenital heart disease, and only echocardiography names the anatomy; a chest radiograph only supports, and repeating a failed screen delays the study
  6. 1-day-old girl has been cyanotic since birth no murmur echocardiogram shows a severely underdeveloped left ventricle Born at term after an uncomplicated pregnancy Afebrile · oxygen saturation 82% on room air · HR 166/min → Prostaglandin E1 infusion → the ductus and the atrial defect are the only route to the systemic circulation, so the shunts must stay open: prostaglandin E1 keeps the ductus open; indomethacin closes it, and oxygen alone leaves it to close over days
  7. 3-week-old girl is seen for a weight check fixed splitting of S2 soft systolic murmur at the left upper sternal border Thriving and gaining weight Afebrile · oxygen saturation 98% on room air → Atrial septal defect → a fixed split S2 with a soft pulmonic flow murmur and no cyanosis is an atrial septal defect; the atrial gradient stays low, so it is often silent into childhood. A ventricular septal defect is holosystolic at the lower sternal border, and a patent ductus is continuous and machine-like
  8. 2-month-old boy was diagnosed with tetralogy of Fallot at birth deeply cyanotic while crying improves when his mother holds his knees to his chest Afebrile · oxygen saturation 62% while crying, 84% after → Increased systemic vascular resistance reduces right-to-left shunting → knee-chest raises systemic vascular resistance, which reverses the right-to-left shunt; the lever is systemic vascular resistance, not venous return or the coronary circulation
  9. 2-month-old girl is evaluated for a murmur holosystolic tricuspid regurgitation murmur at the left lower sternal border widely split S1 early systolic sail sound Feeding and growing well Afebrile · oxygen saturation 92% on room air → Ebstein anomaly → apical displacement of the tricuspid valve atrializes the right ventricle and makes the regurgitation murmur, the widely split S1 and the sail sound; tricuspid atresia has no right atrium to right ventricle path, and pulmonic stenosis makes an outflow murmur
  10. 4-month-old girl was diagnosed with a large ventricular septal defect at 1 month never repaired murmur has softened now desaturates with crying Parents say the quieter murmur means it is closing Afebrile · oxygen saturation 88% at rest → Urgent cardiology referral → a softening murmur in an unrepaired large shunt is a warning, not an improvement: it can mean pulmonary vascular resistance is rising and the shunt is starting to reverse, the road to Eisenmenger syndrome; refer urgently while repair is still possible. Reassurance reads it as closure; an afterload reducer with a 3-month recheck treats overcirculation that is already reversing and delays repair
  11. 1-day-old boy has been cyanotic since birth holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border ECG shows left axis deviation with small right ventricular forces No spells with crying Afebrile · oxygen saturation 78% on room air → Tricuspid atresia → with no right atrium to right ventricle path, flow depends on the atrial defect plus a ventricular defect or ductus, whose murmur is heard; left axis deviation with small right ventricular forces is its ECG. Tetralogy has right ventricular hypertrophy and an outflow murmur. Ebstein, cyanotic at birth when severe, also gives a regurgitation murmur, but adds a widely split S1, a sail sound and a massive box-shaped heart; left axis with small right ventricular forces is the tricuspid atresia ECG
  12. 2-day-old boy is pale and mottled weak femoral pulses right arm blood pressure 30 mm Hg above the leg In shock on arrival Afebrile · BP 86/50 mm Hg in the right arm · HR 190/min → Start prostaglandin E1 → coarctation declares in days, as the ductus closes: prostaglandin E1 reopens it. Diuretics and a fluid bolus leave the closing ductus untouched
  13. 2-month-old boy has cyanosis that began in recent weeks holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border echocardiogram shows a single arterial trunk over a large defect in the ventricular septum Afebrile · oxygen saturation 86% → Truncus arteriosus → a single shared arterial trunk over a ventricular septal defect gives cyanosis characteristically in infancy, not at birth, with a holosystolic murmur; tetralogy has a harsh outflow murmur and spells, and total anomalous pulmonary venous return has no murmur
  14. 3-month-old girl was diagnosed with a ventricular septal defect at 2 weeks loud grade 4/6 holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border echocardiogram shows a small defect Afebrile · weight at the 50th percentile → A small defect produces high-velocity turbulent flow → a small defect makes high-velocity turbulent flow; large defects are quieter and shunt more, so murmur intensity runs opposite to severity. A loud murmur reflects a high gradient, not a high right ventricular pressure, which would soften it
  15. 3-month-old girl has episodes of deeper cyanosis with crying episodes resolve when she is calm harsh systolic ejection murmur at the left upper sternal border Afebrile · baseline oxygen saturation 86% → Echocardiography → echocardiography confirms the ventricular septal defect, overriding aorta and narrowed outflow tract; a chest radiograph (boot-shaped heart) and an ECG only support
  16. 3-day-old preterm boy born at 28 weeks continuous murmur below the left clavicle bounding pulses widened pulse pressure Murmur first heard today on rounds Afebrile · BP 58/24 mm Hg · respiratory rate 64/min → Indomethacin or ibuprofen → a hemodynamically significant preterm ductus (bounding pulses, wide pulse pressure, tachypnea) shunting into the lungs is the problem, so close it with indomethacin or ibuprofen; prostaglandin E1 keeps a ductus open, and observation alone leaves the shunt in place
  17. 2-day-old girl with Down syndrome has a murmur grade 2/6 systolic murmur at the left lower sternal border single loud S2 Feeding well; echocardiography is ordered before discharge Afebrile · oxygen saturation 96% on room air → Complete atrioventricular canal defect → most children with the complete form of atrioventricular septal defect have Down syndrome; the single loud S2 reflects pulmonary hypertension, and heart failure follows by 4 to 6 weeks. Tetralogy of Fallot is linked to 22q11.2 deletion and fetal alcohol syndrome, and coarctation to Turner syndrome
  18. 3-day-old girl has cyanosis unimproved on 100% oxygen single S2 now weak pulses with poor perfusion Born at term after an uncomplicated pregnancy; feeding poorly today Afebrile · oxygen saturation 70% on 100% oxygen · HR 190/min → Start prostaglandin E1 and obtain echocardiography → unchanged saturation on 100% oxygen is a fixed shunt, not lung disease; weak pulses mean the ductus is closing, so instability licenses prostaglandin E1 before the picture; waiting for echocardiography or adding oxygen lets it close
  19. 3-month-old girl was diagnosed with tetralogy of Fallot at birth harsh systolic murmur at the left upper sternal border echocardiogram shows a large ventricular septal defect and an overriding aorta Afebrile · oxygen saturation 88% → Flow through the narrowed RV outflow tract → the ventricular septal defect is real anatomy but too large to generate a murmur; the murmur comes from the narrowed right ventricular (RV) outflow tract, and the overriding aorta adds none
  20. 6-week-old boy has fed poorly for 1 week tachypneic and acyanotic holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border Murmur absent on the newborn examination; born at term Afebrile · respiratory rate 68/min · oxygen saturation 98% → Ventricular septal defect → a holosystolic lower-sternal-border murmur in an acyanotic infant is a ventricular septal defect, appearing as pulmonary vascular resistance falls; an atrial septal defect gives a fixed split S2 and is often silent into childhood, and a patent ductus is continuous
How NBME framed it: question 1

3-month-old boy brought to the emergency department with 3 days of pallor, low-grade fever, vomiting, occasional diarrhea and poor feeding Mildly dehydrated and cyanotic; perfusion and muscle tone normal T 37.8 °C · pulse 165/min · respirations 35/min · BP 80/48 mm Hg · oxygen saturation 85% on room air harsh grade 3/6 systolic ejection murmur over the whole precordium cries and becomes agitated as an intravenous catheter is attempted saturation then drops to 60% and the murmur is barely audible Supplemental oxygen is given

Most likely diagnosis?

Competing answers
  • Atrial septal defect: a common defect with a systolic murmur; but it shunts left to right with a fixed split S2 and causes no cyanosis.
  • Coarctation of the aorta: a can't-miss lesion in an ill infant; but it gives arm hypertension, weak leg pulses and lower leg pressures, not cyanotic spells.
  • Ventricular septal defect: a harsh murmur in an infant; but an isolated defect is holosystolic and acyanotic; a murmur that fades as cyanosis develops over months can mean rising resistance reversing the shunt, the road to Eisenmenger syndrome, not an acute spell with crying.

Down to two: tetralogy of Fallot or pulmonary stenosis. Tetralogy of Fallot: isolated pulmonary stenosis makes a similar outflow murmur, but with no ventricular septal defect it causes no cyanotic spells with crying. Crying tightens the outflow obstruction (the trigger is not fully understood), pulmonary flow drops, and less flow makes a softer murmur. The stem reads like a febrile stomach illness; the witnessed spell names the lesion, and the oxygen given treats the number, not the shunt.

Common wrong answers Oxygen alone in a spell: it is given, but the shunt is anatomic; knee-chest raises systemic vascular resistance, the lever. Flow across the ventricular septal defect: real anatomy, wrong source of the tetralogy murmur. Ductal closure: removes a continuous murmur, cannot create a holosystolic one. Rising pulmonary pressure: the opposite direction; it would soften the murmur.
Pairs with Heart Murmurs in a Child: central cyanosis and a single or fixed S2 are pathologic; ask, cyanosis at birth, and is there a murmur? Cyanosis in the Newborn: the sort to finish first. Heart Murmurs in an Adult: murmur shape and location. Lung Disease in the Newborn and Preterm Infant: lung versus heart.
Transferable rule

Time it, then hear it: when did cyanosis or the murmur arrive, and which structure makes the sound? A murmur that appears or fades means the gradient changed, not the heart.
